function.name: generate_report
function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

**Ionisation methods – a quick guide** | Ionisation technique | Typical application | Key advantages | Common limitations | |----------------------|---------------------|----------------|--------------------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | Gas‑phase mass spectrometry (GC‑MS) | • Simple, robust;
• Produces reproducible fragmentation patterns;
• Good for volatile, thermally stable compounds | • Requires vacuum;
• Not suitable for large, labile molecules;
• Generates many fragment ions (hard ionisation) | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | GC‑MS, some LC‑MS | • Softer than EI → less fragmentation;
• Useful for larger, polar molecules | • Still requires gas phase;
• Ionisation efficiency depends on reagent gas | | **Photoionisation (PI)** | GC‑MS, some LC‑MS | • Very soft;
• Can ionise non‑polar compounds;
• Minimal fragmentation | • Requires UV source;
• Lower sensitivity for some analytes | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | LC‑MS, proteomics, metabolomics | • Soft, produces multiply charged ions → high‑molecular‑weight species detectable;
• Works with aqueous solutions;
• Compatible with high‑throughput workflows | • Suppression effects in complex matrices;
• Requires careful tuning of solvent composition | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteomics, polymers, large biomolecules | • Very soft;
• Handles large biomolecules (proteins, DNA);
• Fast analysis | • Requires matrix;
• Limited to solid samples;
• Quantitation can be challenging | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | LC‑MS, small molecules | • Good for moderately polar, non‑volatile compounds;
• Less matrix effect than ESI | • Not ideal for very polar or large biomolecules | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | LC‑MS, aromatic compounds | • Soft ionisation;
• Good for non‑polar, aromatic species | • Requires UV lamp;
• Less common than ESI/APCI | | **Fast Atom Bombardment (FAB)** | LC‑MS, polar, non‑volatile compounds | • Soft ionisation;
• Works with aqueous solutions | • Less common; requires special source | | **Laser Ablation Electrospray Ionisation (LAESI)** | Imaging, tissue analysis | • Direct sampling of solids/liquids;
• Spatially resolved | • Requires laser source;
• Lower sensitivity than ESI | ### How to choose the “best” method? 1. **Sample type & state** - *Volatile, thermally stable*: EI or CI (GC‑MS). - *Large biomolecules (proteins, peptides)*: MALDI or ESI. - *Polar, non‑volatile*: ESI or APCI (LC‑MS). - *Non‑polar, aromatic*: APPI or PI. 2. **Desired information** - *Structural elucidation*: Hard ionisation (EI) gives rich fragmentation. - *Molecular weight determination*: Soft ionisation (ESI, MALDI) preserves the intact ion. 3. **Matrix effects & quantitation** - ESI is prone to ion suppression in complex matrices; APCI/APPI can mitigate this. - MALDI is less quantitative but excellent for imaging. 4. **Instrumentation & workflow** - If you already have a GC‑MS, EI/CI are natural choices. - For LC‑MS labs, ESI/APCI/APPI are standard. - For rapid, high‑throughput screening, consider automated ESI sources. 5. **Cost & maintenance** - EI/CI sources are relatively inexpensive and low‑maintenance. - MALDI requires matrix preparation and laser maintenance. - ESI/APCI/APPI need careful solvent optimisation. --- #### Bottom line There isn’t a single “best” ionisation method; the optimal choice depends on: - **What you’re analysing** (size, polarity, volatility). - **What information you need** (mass, structure, imaging). - **Your existing instrumentation** and workflow constraints. If you can tell me more about your sample type, analytical goals, and available equipment, I can give a more tailored recommendation.
